1	"""YOLO11l as a TensorRT FP16 engine: building it, and running it.
2	
3	Why: the GPU is the bottleneck (busy ~93% of the run), and TensorRT runs the
4	same network much faster than PyTorch by fusing layers and picking the
5	fastest kernels for this exact GPU.
6	
7	How it is made (once, in prepare.py, on the machine that will run it,
8	because an engine only works on the GPU model and TensorRT version that
9	built it):
10	
11	  yolo11l.pt --Ultralytics export--> yolo11l.onnx --TensorRT build--> yolo11l.engine
12	
13	We build the engine ourselves rather than with Ultralytics' `format="engine"`
14	export because that one tunes the engine for 640x640 inputs, while 3 of 4
15	FineVideo frames letterbox to 640 wide x 384 high. Here the engine is tuned
16	for 384x640 and accepts any size up to 640x640 and any batch up to
17	MAX_BATCH.
18	
19	The engine takes the same input as the PyTorch model (a float tensor
20	(B, 3, H, W), RGB, 0..1) and returns the same raw output (B, 84, anchors),
21	so Ultralytics' non_max_suppression is applied to it unchanged.
22	"""
23	
24	import torch
25	
26	from .config import IMAGE_SIZE
27	
28	MAX_BATCH = 64
29	TUNED_SHAPE = (384, IMAGE_SIZE)          # (H, W) of the most common frames
30	MAX_SHAPE = (IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE)     # letterboxing never exceeds 640 per side
31	MIN_SIDE = 32                            # the model's stride
32	
33	
34	def export_onnx(weights_path):
35	    """yolo11l.pt -> yolo11l.onnx with dynamic batch, height and width."""
36	    from ultralytics import YOLO
37	
38	    onnx_path = YOLO(str(weights_path)).export(
39	        format="onnx", dynamic=True, simplify=True, imgsz=IMAGE_SIZE
40	    )
41	    return onnx_path
42	
43	
44	def build_engine(onnx_path, engine_path):
45	    """Build an FP16 TensorRT engine from the ONNX file. Takes a few minutes."""
46	    import tensorrt as trt
47	
48	    logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)
49	    builder = trt.Builder(logger)
50	    network = builder.create_network(0)
51	    parser = trt.OnnxParser(network, logger)
52	    if not parser.parse_from_file(str(onnx_path)):
53	        errors = [str(parser.get_error(i)) for i in range(parser.num_errors)]
54	        raise RuntimeError("could not parse ONNX: " + "; ".join(errors))
55	
56	    config = builder.create_builder_config()
57	    config.set_flag(trt.BuilderFlag.FP16)  # layers run in FP16; inputs/outputs stay FP32
58	    config.set_memory_pool_limit(trt.MemoryPoolType.WORKSPACE, 4 << 30)
59	
60	    # One optimization profile covering every input this pipeline can send.
61	    profile = builder.create_optimization_profile()
62	    name = network.get_input(0).name
63	    profile.set_shape(
64	        name,
65	        min=(1, 3, MIN_SIDE, MIN_SIDE),
66	        opt=(MAX_BATCH, 3, *TUNED_SHAPE),
67	        max=(MAX_BATCH, 3, *MAX_SHAPE),
68	    )
69	    config.add_optimization_profile(profile)
70	
71	    serialized = builder.build_serialized_network(network, config)
72	    if serialized is None:
73	        raise RuntimeError("TensorRT engine build failed")
74	    with open(engine_path, "wb") as f:
75	        f.write(serialized)
76

78	class TrtModel:
79	    """Runs a built engine on CUDA torch tensors, as a drop-in for the
80	    PyTorch model's forward pass."""
81	
82	    def __init__(self, engine_path, device):
83	        import tensorrt as trt
84	
85	        self.device = device
86	        logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)
87	        with open(engine_path, "rb") as f:
88	            self.engine = trt.Runtime(logger).deserialize_cuda_engine(f.read())
89	        if self.engine is None:
90	            raise RuntimeError(f"could not load TensorRT engine {engine_path}")
91	        self.context = self.engine.create_execution_context()
92	
93	        names = [self.engine.get_tensor_name(i) for i in range(self.engine.num_io_tensors)]
94	        self.input_name = next(n for n in names if self.engine.get_tensor_mode(n) == trt.TensorIOMode.INPUT)
95	        self.output_name = next(n for n in names if self.engine.get_tensor_mode(n) == trt.TensorIOMode.OUTPUT)
96	
97	    def __call__(self, x):
98	        """x: float tensor (B, 3, H, W) on the GPU, B <= MAX_BATCH, H and W <= 640."""
99	        x = x.float().contiguous()
100	        self.context.set_input_shape(self.input_name, tuple(x.shape))
101	        out = torch.empty(
102	            tuple(self.context.get_tensor_shape(self.output_name)), dtype=torch.float32, device=self.device
103	        )
104	        self.context.set_tensor_address(self.input_name, x.data_ptr())
105	        self.context.set_tensor_address(self.output_name, out.data_ptr())
106	        # Run on PyTorch's current CUDA stream, so the work is ordered with
107	        # the preprocessing before it and the NMS after it.
108	        if not self.context.execute_async_v3(torch.cuda.current_stream(self.device).cuda_stream):
109	            raise RuntimeError("TensorRT execution failed")
110	        return out

(B, 3, H, W), RGB, 0..1) and returns the same raw output (B, 84, anchors),
so Ultralytics' non_max_suppression is applied to it unchanged.
"""

import torch

from .config import IMAGE_SIZE

MAX_BATCH = 64
TUNED_SHAPE = (384, IMAGE_SIZE)          # (H, W) of the most common frames
MAX_SHAPE = (IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE)     # letterboxing never exceeds 640 per side
MIN_SIDE = 32                            # the model's stride


def export_onnx(weights_path):
    """yolo11l.pt -> yolo11l.onnx with dynamic batch, height and width."""
    from ultralytics import YOLO

    onnx_path = YOLO(str(weights_path)).export(
        format="onnx", dynamic=True, simplify=True, imgsz=IMAGE_SIZE
    )
    return onnx_path


def build_engine(onnx_path, engine_path):
    """Build an FP16 TensorRT engine from the ONNX file. Takes a few minutes."""
    import tensorrt as trt

    logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)
    builder = trt.Builder(logger)
    network = builder.create_network(0)
    parser = trt.OnnxParser(network, logger)
    if not parser.parse_from_file(str(onnx_path)):
        errors = [str(parser.get_error(i)) for i in range(parser.num_errors)]
        raise RuntimeError("could not parse ONNX: " + "; ".join(errors))

    config = builder.create_builder_config()
    config.set_flag(trt.BuilderFlag.FP16)  # layers run in FP16; inputs/outputs stay FP32
    config.set_memory_pool_limit(trt.MemoryPoolType.WORKSPACE, 4 << 30)

    # One optimization profile covering every input this pipeline can send.
    profile = builder.create_optimization_profile()
    name = network.get_input(0).name
    profile.set_shape(
        name,
        min=(1, 3, MIN_SIDE, MIN_SIDE),
        opt=(MAX_BATCH, 3, *TUNED_SHAPE),
        max=(MAX_BATCH, 3, *MAX_SHAPE),
    )
    config.add_optimization_profile(profile)

    serialized = builder.build_serialized_network(network, config)
    if serialized is None:
        raise RuntimeError("TensorRT engine build failed")
    with open(engine_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(serialized)


class TrtModel:
    """Runs a built engine on CUDA torch tensors, as a drop-in for the
    PyTorch model's forward pass."""

    def __init__(self, engine_path, device):
        import tensorrt as trt

        self.device = device
        logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)
        with open(engine_path, "rb") as f:
            self.engine = trt.Runtime(logger).deserialize_cuda_engine(f.read())
        if self.engine is None:
            raise RuntimeError(f"could not load TensorRT engine {engine_path}")
        self.context = self.engine.create_execution_context()

        names = [self.engine.get_tensor_name(i) for i in range(self.engine.num_io_tensors)]
        self.input_name = next(n for n in names if self.engine.get_tensor_mode(n) == trt.TensorIOMode.INPUT)
        self.output_name = next(n for n in names if self.engine.get_tensor_mode(n) == trt.TensorIOMode.OUTPUT)

    def __call__(self, x):
        """x: float tensor (B, 3, H, W) on the GPU, B <= MAX_BATCH, H and W <= 640."""
        x = x.float().contiguous()
        self.context.set_input_shape(self.input_name, tuple(x.shape))
        out = torch.empty(
            tuple(self.context.get_tensor_shape(self.output_name)), dtype=torch.float32, device=self.device
        )
        self.context.set_tensor_address(self.input_name, x.data_ptr())
        self.context.set_tensor_address(self.output_name, out.data_ptr())
        # Run on PyTorch's current CUDA stream, so the work is ordered with
        # the preprocessing before it and the NMS after it.
        if not self.context.execute_async_v3(torch.cuda.current_stream(self.device).cuda_stream):
            raise RuntimeError("TensorRT execution failed")
        return out

1	"""YOLO11l on batches of frames, returning per-frame object counts.
2	
3	Ultralytics' own predict() does the same work, one Python call per batch with
4	CPU-side preprocessing and Results objects we do not need. Here we do just:
5	
6	  1. letterbox on the CPU, in the decode workers (`make_letterbox`), using
7	     Ultralytics' own LetterBox class so the model input is identical to
8	     what predict() would build;
9	  2. on the GPU: BGR->RGB, HWC->CHW, uint8 -> float, /255;
10	  3. the model forward pass: a TensorRT FP16 engine if prepare.py built
11	     one (see trt_engine.py), otherwise the PyTorch model in fp16;
12	  4. NMS with the brief's settings: a batched re-implementation of
13	     Ultralytics' non_max_suppression (see batched_nms_counts);
14	  5. count detections per target class per frame.
15	
16	Steps 2 and 4 mirror ultralytics/engine/predictor.py `preprocess` and
17	ultralytics/utils/nms.py `non_max_suppression`.
18	"""
19	
20	import sys
21	
22	import torch
23	import torchvision
24	from ultralytics import YOLO
25	from ultralytics.data.augment import LetterBox
26	
27	from .config import CLASS_IDS, CONFIDENCE, ENGINE, IMAGE_SIZE, NMS_IOU, WEIGHTS
28	
29	# yolo11l.pt has a maximum stride of 32; predict() letterboxes to a multiple of it.
30	MODEL_STRIDE = 32
31	
32	
33	def make_letterbox():
34	    """The same resize-and-pad predict() applies to a batch of equal-size frames.
35	
36	    auto=True pads only up to the next multiple of the stride (a 640x360
37	    frame becomes 640x384, not 640x640). That is what predict() does for a
38	    .pt model when every image in the batch has the same shape, which is
39	    always true for frames of one video.
40	    """
41	    return LetterBox(new_shape=(IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE), auto=True, stride=MODEL_STRIDE)
42	
43	
44	class Detector:
45	    """backend: "tensorrt", "pytorch", or "auto" (TensorRT if the engine
46	    file exists and loads, otherwise PyTorch)."""
47	
48	    def __init__(self, device="cuda:0", half=True, backend="auto", weights=WEIGHTS, engine=ENGINE):
49	        self.device = torch.device(device)
50	        self.half = half
51	        self.backend = None
52	
53	        if backend in ("auto", "tensorrt"):
54	            try:
55	                from .trt_engine import TrtModel
56	
57	                self.model = TrtModel(engine, self.device)
58	                self.backend = "tensorrt"
59	            except Exception as exc:
60	                if backend == "tensorrt":
61	                    raise
62	                print(f"TensorRT engine not used ({type(exc).__name__}: {exc}); "
63	                      f"falling back to PyTorch", file=sys.stderr)
64	
65	        if self.backend is None:
66	            model = YOLO(str(weights)).model  # the underlying torch nn.Module
67	            model = model.fuse(verbose=False)  # predict() also fuses Conv+BN
68	            model = model.to(self.device).eval()
69	            if half:
70	                model = model.half()
71	            self.model = model
72	            self.backend = "pytorch-fp16" if half else "pytorch-fp32"
73	
74	        # TensorRT's engine takes float32 input (it computes in FP16 inside);
75	        # the PyTorch model takes whatever precision its weights are in.
76	        self.input_dtype = torch.float16 if self.backend == "pytorch-fp16" else torch.float32
77	
78	        self.stream = torch.cuda.Stream(self.device)
79	
80	        # Lookup: COCO class id -> column (0..4) in our count rows.
81	        self._column_of_class = torch.full((256,), -1, dtype=torch.long, device=self.device)
82	        for column, class_id in enumerate(CLASS_IDS):
83	            self._column_of_class[class_id] = column
84	
85	    def count_objects(self, frames):
86	        """frames: uint8 tensor (B, H, W, 3), letterboxed, BGR, on any device.
87	
88	        Returns an int64 CPU tensor (B, 5): for each frame, how many of each
89	        target object were detected with confidence >= CONFIDENCE.
90	
91	        If the GPU runs out of memory (it happened on a shared development
92	        GPU), the batch is split in half and retried, down to one frame,
93	        instead of failing the whole run. Results are the same either way:
94	        each frame is processed independently.
95	        """
96	        try:
97	            # A stream of our own: TensorRT adds extra synchronisation when
98	            # it is given CUDA's default stream.
99	            with torch.cuda.stream(self.stream):
100	                return self._count_batch(frames)
101	        except torch.OutOfMemoryError:
102	            if len(frames) == 1:
103	                raise
104	            torch.cuda.empty_cache()
105	            half = len(frames) // 2
106	            return torch.cat([self.count_objects(frames[:half]), self.count_objects(frames[half:])])
107	
108	    @torch.inference_mode()
109	    def _count_batch(self, frames):
110	        x = frames.to(self.device, non_blocking=True)
111	        x = x.flip(-1)                    # BGR -> RGB (the model was trained on RGB)
112	        x = x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2)         # BHWC -> BCHW
113	        x = x.to(self.input_dtype).contiguous() / 255.0
114	
115	        predictions = self.model(x)
116	        return batched_nms_counts(predictions, self._column_of_class).cpu()
117	
118	
119	MAX_DETECTIONS = 300  # per image, Ultralytics' max_det default
120	
121	
122	def batched_nms_counts(predictions, column_of_class):
123	    """NMS for a whole batch in one go, then per-frame counts of our 5 objects.
124	
125	    Gives the same detections as Ultralytics'
126	    `non_max_suppression(predictions, conf_thres=0.4, iou_thres=0.7,
127	    classes=CLASS_IDS, max_det=300)` (ultralytics/utils/nms.py), which loops
128	    over the images in Python and took as long as the model itself
129	    (26.8 ms vs 26.1 ms for a batch of 64). This does the same steps for all
130	    images at once:
131	
132	      1. each box takes its single best class over ALL 80 COCO classes
133	         (multi_label=False), and is kept if that score is > 0.4 (strictly
134	         greater, as in Ultralytics) and that class is one of our five;
135	      2. class-aware NMS at IoU 0.7: boxes only suppress boxes of the same
136	         class IN THE SAME IMAGE, so the NMS group is (image, class);
137	         torchvision's batched_nms is the same torchvision NMS Ultralytics
138	         calls, with the same coordinate-offset trick to keep groups apart;
139	      3. at most 300 detections per image, highest scores first.
140	
141	    tools/test_nms.py checks the counts against Ultralytics on real frames.
142	
143	    predictions: raw model output (B, 4 + 80, anchors), boxes as center x,
144	                 center y, width, height (or a tuple whose first item is that).
145	    Returns an int64 tensor (B, 5) on the predictions' device.
146	    """
147	    if isinstance(predictions, (list, tuple)):
148	        predictions = predictions[0]
149	    n_images = predictions.shape[0]
150	    n_columns = int((column_of_class >= 0).sum())
151	    pred = predictions.transpose(1, 2)            # (B, anchors, 84)
152	
153	    # 1. best class per box, then the confidence and class filters
154	    best_score, best_class = pred[..., 4:].max(dim=-1)
155	    keep = (best_score > CONFIDENCE) & (column_of_class[best_class] >= 0)
156	    image, anchor = keep.nonzero(as_tuple=True)
157	    if image.numel() == 0:
158	        return torch.zeros((n_images, n_columns), dtype=torch.long, device=pred.device)
159	
160	    boxes = xywh2xyxy(pred[image, anchor, :4])
161	    scores = best_score[image, anchor]
162	    classes = best_class[image, anchor]
163	
164	    # 2. one NMS call for every (image, class) group at once
165	    n_classes = pred.shape[-1] - 4
166	    groups = image * n_classes + classes
167	    kept = torchvision.ops.batched_nms(boxes.float(), scores.float(), groups, NMS_IOU)  # sorted by score, high first
168	    kept_image = image[kept]
169	
170	    # 3. cap each image at MAX_DETECTIONS, keeping its highest scores: group
171	    #    the kept boxes by image (a stable sort keeps the score order inside
172	    #    each image) and number them 0, 1, 2, ... within their image.
173	    order = torch.argsort(kept_image, stable=True)
174	    sorted_image = kept_image[order]
175	    first_of_image = torch.searchsorted(sorted_image, sorted_image)
176	    rank = torch.arange(len(order), device=pred.device) - first_of_image
177	    kept = kept[order[rank < MAX_DETECTIONS]]
178	
179	    # Count per (image, column).
180	    flat = image[kept] * n_columns + column_of_class[classes[kept]]
181	    counts = torch.bincount(flat, minlength=n_images * n_columns)
182	    return counts.view(n_images, n_columns)
183	
184	
185	def xywh2xyxy(xywh):
186	    """(center x, center y, width, height) -> (x1, y1, x2, y2), as in Ultralytics."""
187	    xy, wh = xywh[..., :2], xywh[..., 2:] / 2
188	    return torch.cat((xy - wh, xy + wh), dim=-1)

    flip) on uint8 data but accepts a Cast from uint8. The result is the
    same arithmetic as the PyTorch path in detector.preprocess().
    \"\"\"

        helper.make_node("Transpose", ["frames_float"], ["frames_chw"], perm=[0, 3, 1, 2]),
        helper.make_node("Gather", ["frames_chw", "bgr_to_rgb"], ["frames_rgb"], axis=1),
        helper.make_node("Div", ["frames_rgb", "pixel_scale"], [model_input]),

    graph.input.insert(0, frames)

content.text:
The preprocessing is now part of the engine, and it gives the same results as before. A fresh full run is going in the background so the submitted results and timing come from this exact version.

## #2: preprocessing inside the ONNX and engine

The engine now takes the letterboxed frames as the decode workers produce them: `uint8 (batch, H, W, 3)`, BGR. Four nodes in front of YOLO do the rest ([add_preprocessing](videoindex/trt_engine.py)):

```
frames (uint8 BGR) → Cast float32 → Transpose to (B,3,H,W) → Gather [2,1,0] (BGR→RGB) → ÷255 → YOLO11l
```

The Cast comes first because TensorRT rejects a channel flip on `uint8`. `prepare.py` now goes `.pt → .onnx → _preprocessed.onnx → .engine`. The PyTorch fallback keeps the same steps in Python (`preprocess()`), and the engine refuses an old float-input engine file.

**Checks:**
- **The ONNX graph change is exact:** run in ONNX Runtime, the new ONNX on raw frames and the old ONNX with Python preprocessing give a **max difference of 0.0**.
- **Accuracy vs the every-frame reference is unchanged:** F1 0.9830, exact 94.01%, within ±1 99.59%. The NMS test still shows 0 differences from Ultralytics.
- **Speed: 37.5 s vs 37.7 s**, no real change, as predicted, since these steps were only about 0.8 ms of a 30 ms batch. What you get is the cleaner engine contract.
- Against the previous engine, results agree on 99.97% of objects. They're not byte-identical, because every TensorRT build picks its fastest FP16 kernels by timing them, which isn't deterministic.

## How the NMS works, and where it runs

**It all runs on the GPU.** The only data that reaches the CPU is the final counts table: 64 frames × 5 numbers per batch.

[batched_nms_counts](videoindex/detector.py) takes the model's raw output for a batch, shape `(64, 84, anchors)`: for each of about 5,040 candidate boxes per frame (at 640×384), 4 box numbers plus 80 class scores. Then:

1. **Best class per box.** Each box takes its highest-scoring class across all 80 COCO classes. It's kept only if that score is > 0.4 and the class is one of our five. A box whose best class is "truck" is dropped, even if its "car" score is also high. This is exactly Ultralytics' rule.
2. **Class-aware NMS in one call.** The surviving boxes from all 64 frames go into a single `torchvision.ops.batched_nms` call, at IoU 0.7. Each box gets a group number, `frame × 80 + class`, so a box can only suppress boxes of the same class in the same frame.
3. **At most 300 detections per frame**, highest scores first. This is the Ultralytics default and rarely matters.
4. **Counting.** One `bincount` turns the kept boxes into the `(64, 5)` counts table, which is then copied to the CPU.

**Why I rewrote it.** Ultralytics' `non_max_suppression` also runs on the GPU, but it loops over the 64 frames in Python and starts many small GPU operations per frame. That overhead cost **26.8 ms per batch, as much as the model itself (26.1 ms)**. The batched version does the same thing in a handful of operations for the whole batch. `tools/test_nms.py` checks it against Ultralytics on 512 real frames, for both TensorRT and PyTorch, with **0 differences**.

**Could NMS go inside the engine too?** Yes, TensorRT has an NMS plugin (`EfficientNMS`), but its rules differ from Ultralytics' (how classes are chosen, edge cases), so I'd have to prove it matches all over again for a gain of 1–2 ms per batch. It isn't worth it today.

## Still to do
- **Full run with the new engine** (about 17 min, background). When it finishes, `results.jsonl.gz` is rewritten automatically, and I'll update `HARDWARE.md` with the time.
- **`WRITEUP.md`**, written by you.
- **Chat logs:** redaction, and your decision on the `CLAUDE.md` content.
- **GitHub repo:** I'll show you the commit and wait for your approval before pushing.

"""YOLO11l as a TensorRT FP16 engine: building it, and running it.

Why: the GPU is the bottleneck (busy ~93% of the run), and TensorRT runs the
same network much faster than PyTorch by fusing layers and picking the
fastest kernels for this exact GPU.

How it is made (once, in prepare.py, on the machine that will run it,
because an engine only works on the GPU model and TensorRT version that
built it):

  yolo11l.pt --Ultralytics export--> yolo11l.onnx
             --add preprocessing-->  yolo11l_preprocessed.onnx
             --TensorRT build-->     yolo11l.engine

We build the engine ourselves rather than with Ultralytics' `format="engine"`
export because that one tunes the engine for 640x640 inputs, while 3 of 4
FineVideo frames letterbox to 640 wide x 384 high. Here the engine is tuned
for 384x640 and accepts any size up to 640x640 and any batch up to
MAX_BATCH.

The preprocessing is part of the engine: it takes the letterboxed frames
exactly as the decode workers produce them, uint8 (B, H, W, 3) in BGR
order, and does uint8 -> float, HWC -> CHW, BGR -> RGB and /255 itself
(`add_preprocessing`). It returns the same raw output as the PyTorch model,
(B, 84, anchors), which goes to the same NMS.
"""

import torch

from .config import IMAGE_SIZE

MAX_BATCH = 64
TUNED_SHAPE = (384, IMAGE_SIZE)          # (H, W) of the most common frames
MAX_SHAPE = (IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE)     # letterboxing never exceeds 640 per side
MIN_SIDE = 32                            # the model's stride


def export_onnx(weights_path):
    """yolo11l.pt -> yolo11l.onnx with dynamic batch, height and width."""
    from ultralytics import YOLO

    onnx_path = YOLO(str(weights_path)).export(
        format="onnx", dynamic=True, simplify=True, imgsz=IMAGE_SIZE
    )
    return onnx_path


def add_preprocessing(onnx_path, out_path):
    """Put the input preprocessing inside the ONNX graph.

    New input "frames": uint8 (batch, height, width, 3), BGR. Four nodes turn
    it into what the exported model expects as "images" (float32
    (batch, 3, height, width), RGB, 0..1):

        Cast(float32) -> Transpose(to B,3,H,W) -> Gather([2,1,0]) -> Div(255)

    The Cast comes FIRST on purpose: TensorRT rejects a Gather (the channel
    flip) on uint8 data but accepts a Cast from uint8. The result is the
    same arithmetic as the PyTorch path in detector.preprocess().
    """
    import numpy as np
    import onnx
    from onnx import TensorProto, helper, numpy_helper

    model = onnx.load(str(onnx_path))
    graph = model.graph
    old_input = graph.input[0]  # "images", float32 (batch, 3, height, width)
    model_input = old_input.name

    frames = helper.make_tensor_value_info("frames", TensorProto.UINT8, ["batch", "height", "width", 3])
    constants = [
        numpy_helper.from_array(np.array([2, 1, 0], dtype=np.int64), "bgr_to_rgb"),
        numpy_helper.from_array(np.array(255.0, dtype=np.float32), "pixel_scale"),
    ]
    preprocessing = [
        helper.make_node("Cast", ["frames"], ["frames_float"], to=TensorProto.FLOAT),
        helper.make_node("Transpose", ["frames_float"], ["frames_chw"], perm=[0, 3, 1, 2]),
        helper.make_node("Gather", ["frames_chw", "bgr_to_rgb"], ["frames_rgb"], axis=1),
        helper.make_node("Div", ["frames_rgb", "pixel_scale"], [model_input]),
    ]

    graph.input.remove(old_input)
    graph.input.insert(0, frames)
    graph.initializer.extend(constants)
    nodes = preprocessing + list(graph.node)  # new nodes first: the graph must stay in order
    graph.ClearField("node")
    graph.node.extend(nodes)

    onnx.checker.check_model(model)
    onnx.save(model, str(out_path))
    return out_path


def build_engine(onnx_path, engine_path):
    """Build an FP16 TensorRT engine from the ONNX file. Takes a few minutes."""
    import tensorrt as trt

    logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)
    builder = trt.Builder(logger)
    network = builder.create_network(0)
    parser = trt.OnnxParser(network, logger)
    if not parser.parse_from_file(str(onnx_path)):
        errors = [str(parser.get_error(i)) for i in range(parser.num_errors)]
        raise RuntimeError("could not parse ONNX: " + "; ".join(errors))

    config = builder.create_builder_config()
    config.set_flag(trt.BuilderFlag.FP16)  # layers run in FP16; input uint8, output FP32
    config.set_memory_pool_limit(trt.MemoryPoolType.WORKSPACE, 4 << 30)

    # One optimization profile covering every input this pipeline can send.
    # Shapes are (batch, height, width, 3): the frames as the workers send them.
    profile = builder.create_optimization_profile()
    name = network.get_input(0).name
    profile.set_shape(
        name,
        min=(1, MIN_SIDE, MIN_SIDE, 3),
        opt=(MAX_BATCH, *TUNED_SHAPE, 3),
        max=(MAX_BATCH, *MAX_SHAPE, 3),
    )
    config.add_optimization_profile(profile)

    serialized = builder.build_serialized_network(network, config)
    if serialized is None:
        raise RuntimeError("TensorRT engine build failed")
    with open(engine_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(serialized)


class TrtModel:
    """Runs a built engine on CUDA torch tensors, as a drop-in for the
    PyTorch model's forward pass."""

    def __init__(self, engine_path, device):
        import tensorrt as trt

        self.device = device
        logger = trt.Logger(trt.Logger.WARNING)
        with open(engine_path, "rb") as f:
            self.engine = trt.Runtime(logger).deserialize_cuda_engine(f.read())
        if self.engine is None:
            raise RuntimeError(f"could not load TensorRT engine {engine_path}")
        self.context = self.engine.create_execution_context()

        names = [self.engine.get_tensor_name(i) for i in range(self.engine.num_io_tensors)]
        self.input_name = next(n for n in names if self.engine.get_tensor_mode(n) == trt.TensorIOMode.INPUT)
        self.output_name = next(n for n in names if self.engine.get_tensor_mode(n) == trt.TensorIOMode.OUTPUT)

        # An engine from before the preprocessing was baked in takes float
        # input; refuse it rather than feed it raw pixels.
        if self.engine.get_tensor_dtype(self.input_name) != trt.DataType.UINT8:
            raise RuntimeError("engine does not take uint8 frames; rebuild it with prepare.py")

    def __call__(self, frames):
        """frames: uint8 tensor (B, H, W, 3), letterboxed, BGR, on the GPU.
        B <= MAX_BATCH, H and W <= 640."""
        x = frames.contiguous()
        self.context.set_input_shape(self.input_name, tuple(x.shape))
        out = torch.empty(
            tuple(self.context.get_tensor_shape(self.output_name)), dtype=torch.float32, device=self.device
        )
        self.context.set_tensor_address(self.input_name, x.data_ptr())
        self.context.set_tensor_address(self.output_name, out.data_ptr())
        # Run on PyTorch's current CUDA stream, so the work is ordered with
        # the preprocessing before it and the NMS after it.
        if not self.context.execute_async_v3(torch.cuda.current_stream(self.device).cuda_stream):
            raise RuntimeError("TensorRT execution failed")
        return out

content.text:
While that finishes, here's your NMS question.

## How NMS works here, and where it runs

**It runs entirely on the GPU.** The model's output never leaves the GPU. The only thing copied back to the CPU is the final count table, 64 frames × 5 numbers per batch (a few hundred bytes).

The code is `batched_nms_counts` in [videoindex/detector.py](videoindex/detector.py). For one batch of 64 frames, the model outputs a tensor of shape `(64, 84, 5040)`: for each frame, 5,040 candidate boxes (anchors), each with 4 box coordinates plus 80 class scores. Then:

1. **Best class per box.** Each box takes its single highest-scoring class out of all 80 COCO classes. It's kept only if that score is **> 0.4** and that class is one of our five (person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone). This is one `max` plus a mask over the whole batch. Out of 64 × 5,040 ≈ 322k candidates, typically a few thousand survive.
2. **Overlap removal (NMS) for the whole batch in one call.** Boxes are converted from centre/width/height to corners, and every surviving box gets a group number, `image × 80 + class`. `torchvision.ops.batched_nms` with IoU 0.7 then removes, within each group, any box overlapping a higher-scoring box by more than 70%. Because the group includes the image, boxes only suppress boxes of the **same class in the same frame**. That's the class-aware NMS the brief asks for.
3. **At most 300 detections per frame**, highest scores first, the same as Ultralytics' default (it only matters in extremely crowded scenes).
4. **Counting.** One `bincount` over `(frame, class)` gives the 64 × 5 table, which goes to the CPU for the per-second rules.

**Why I rewrote it:** Ultralytics' `non_max_suppression` does the same steps, also on the GPU, but in a **Python loop over the 64 frames**. That means 64 rounds of small GPU operations, each waiting on Python. It took **26.8 ms per batch, as long as the model itself (26.1 ms)**. The batched version does the whole batch in a handful of GPU calls. It's the same algorithm, using the same torchvision NMS function Ultralytics uses inside, applied to all frames at once.

**Verified:** [tools/test_nms.py](tools/test_nms.py) feeds the same model output to both versions. On 512 real frames the counts are identical, for both backends, and the 300 cap matches on a synthetic crowded frame. The full-pipeline output files were also byte-identical before and after the change.

## #2 so far
- The ONNX now takes raw `uint8` BGR frames `(batch, H, W, 3)` and does Cast, then HWC→CHW, then BGR→RGB, then ÷255 inside. Checked in ONNX Runtime against the old ONNX plus Python preprocessing on real frames: **bit-for-bit identical output** (max difference 0.0).
- The new engine built and loads with a `uint8` input.
- Found and fixed along the way: when the GPU is too full, TensorRT silently returns no execution context. Previously that crashed on the first batch; it now falls back to PyTorch cleanly.
- **Still to check once the GPU is free:** the NMS test and the subset score against the reference with the new engine, plus whether it's faster. I'll report back.

content.text:
#2 is done and verified. The engine now takes the raw letterboxed `uint8` BGR frames and does all the preprocessing itself.

**Checks for the new engine:**
- **The graph is exactly right:** the new ONNX on raw frames gives bit-for-bit the same output as the old ONNX plus Python preprocessing (max difference 0.0).
- **Results:** against the every-frame reference it scores F1 0.983, exact 94.0%, within ±1 99.6%, unchanged and passing. NMS still matches Ultralytics on all 512 test frames.
- **Full 50-file run** (the one that was already running): all 1,650 videos, exit 0. It agrees with the previous engine's full run on 99.97% of objects and 99.89% of people counts; small differences between TensorRT builds are normal.
- **Speed:** about 2% faster (55.5 vs 56.7 ms per batch, timed alternately so both saw the same GPU load). So the gain is the cleaner interface, as expected.
- **Bug found and fixed:** when the GPU is nearly full, TensorRT silently fails to create its working memory, and `run.py` crashed on the first batch instead of falling back to PyTorch. It now falls back.

**The GPU is still at 100% from other jobs on Beast**, even with nothing of ours running. That's why the new engine's full run took **1,332 s** against 1,014 s this morning on the old engine; it's the same code speed, just competing for the GPU.

### Your decision: which run to submit
`results.jsonl.gz` and `HARDWARE.md` currently come from this morning's run (old engine, 1,014 s). The code in the repo now uses the new engine. Options:

1. **Re-run the full 50 files when the GPU is quieter (my recommendation).** It takes about 17 minutes if the GPU is free. Results and timing would then both come from the exact code you submit. I can start it in the background now; whether it finishes uncontended depends on the other jobs.
2. **Submit the 1,332 s run** (`runs/final2_results.jsonl`, new engine). It matches the code, and `HARDWARE.md` would say the GPU was shared.
3. **Keep this morning's results and timing.** They're 99.97% the same, but `HARDWARE.md` would need a note that they came from the build just before the preprocessing moved into the engine.

content.text:
Here's what's on Beast's GPU. I haven't stopped anything:

| What | GPU memory | Real compute load | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **`vllm`** container (vLLM engine) | **20.2 GB** | ~0% while idle; bursts when someone sends requests | Restarted 7 h ago, `restart: unless-stopped` |
| **`3dvt-person-live-*`**: 4 cameras × (imagebuffer, yolo, tracker, drawer) | 4 × ~0.55 GB, plus decoder use | **steady ~15–20% of the GPU's compute**, plus 2–3% of the video decoder | A live 4-camera person-tracking pipeline, up for 5 days |
| **`triton-engine-1`** (Triton) | 3.3 GB | serves the 3dvt `yolo` models | Needed by 3dvt |
| clearml, label-studio, go2rtc, redis, buildkit | none | none | Leave alone |

The "100% utilisation" figure was misleading. That metric means "some kernel was running at every sample". The actual compute load from other jobs is about **15–20%**, all from the live 3dvt pipeline. Power draw is ~113 W of 575 W.

**What would free the GPU for our runs:**
- **The 3dvt live pipeline plus `triton-engine-1`** gives back the steady ~15–20%. This is the one that matters for timing.
- **`vllm`** frees 20 GB of memory, which we don't need (we use about 4 GB), and removes any request bursts. The 1,332 s run was probably slowed by vLLM requests or 3dvt load spikes.

These are team services, so stopping them is your call, and I won't run these myself. If you decide to, the commands are below (run from each service's compose directory if they're compose-managed):
```bash
docker stop $(docker ps -q --filter name=3dvt-person-live) triton-engine-1   # later: docker start <same names>
docker stop vllm                                                              # later: docker start vllm
```

Meanwhile I'll do the README/requirements audit and look for further speed-ups. One promising idea, measured on CPU only so it doesn't disturb anything: many FineVideo videos are static (talking heads, slides), so many sampled frames may be near-identical to the previous one, and their detections could be reused instead of running the model.

"""How many sampled frames are near-copies of the previous sampled frame?

    python tools/measure_duplicates.py <folder of .parquet> [--videos 40]

If many are, the model could be skipped for them and the previous frame's
detections reused. Compares each sampled frame (3 per second) with the
previous one from the same video on a small grayscale thumbnail, and
reports the share of frames below several difference thresholds.
CPU only.
"""

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))
from videoindex.decode import FrameSampler, frame_to_bgr, iter_frames  # noqa: E402

THRESHOLDS = [0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5]  # mean absolute difference, in grey levels (0-255)


def thumbnail(image):
    grey = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    return cv2.resize(grey, (64, 36), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.int16)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("input")
    parser.add_argument("--videos", type=int, default=40)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    diffs = []
    n_videos = 0
    for path in sorted(Path(args.input).glob("*.parquet")):
        column = pq.read_table(path, columns=["mp4"]).column("mp4")
        for row in range(len(column)):
            if n_videos >= args.videos:
                break
            n_videos += 1
            sampler, previous = FrameSampler(3), None
            for t, frame in iter_frames(column[row].as_py()):
                if not sampler.keep(t):
                    continue
                thumb = thumbnail(frame_to_bgr(frame))
                if previous is not None:
                    diffs.append(float(np.abs(thumb - previous).mean()))
                previous = thumb

    diffs = np.array(diffs)
    print(f"{n_videos} videos, {len(diffs)} sampled frames compared with the previous one")
    for threshold in THRESHOLDS:
        print(f"  difference < {threshold:>3} grey levels: {np.mean(diffs < threshold):6.1%} of frames")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""How many sampled frames are near-copies of the previous sampled frame?

    python tools/measure_duplicates.py <folder of .parquet> [--videos 40]

If many are, the model could be skipped for them and the previous frame's
detections reused. Compares each sampled frame (3 per second) with the
previous one from the same video on a small grayscale thumbnail, and
reports the share of frames below several difference thresholds.
CPU only.
"""

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))
from videoindex.decode import FrameSampler, frame_to_bgr, iter_frames  # noqa: E402

THRESHOLDS = [0.5, 1, 2, 3, 5]  # mean absolute difference, in grey levels (0-255)


def thumbnail(image):
    grey = cv2.cvtColor(image, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
    return cv2.resize(grey, (64, 36), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.int16)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("input")
    parser.add_argument("--videos", type=int, default=40)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    diffs = []
    n_videos = 0
    for path in sorted(Path(args.input).glob("*.parquet")):
        column = pq.read_table(path, columns=["mp4"]).column("mp4")
        for row in range(len(column)):
            if n_videos >= args.videos:
                break
            n_videos += 1
            sampler, previous = FrameSampler(3), None
            for t, frame in iter_frames(column[row].as_py()):
                if not sampler.keep(t):
                    continue
                thumb = thumbnail(frame_to_bgr(frame))
                if previous is not None:
                    diffs.append(float(np.abs(thumb - previous).mean()))
                previous = thumb

    diffs = np.array(diffs)
    print(f"{n_videos} videos, {len(diffs)} sampled frames compared with the previous one")
    for threshold in THRESHOLDS:
        print(f"  difference < {threshold:>3} grey levels: {np.mean(diffs < threshold):6.1%} of frames")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Video indexing at speed: FineVideo × YOLO11l

For every second of every video in a folder of FineVideo Parquet files, this
records which of **person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone** appear and how many
people are visible, using Ultralytics YOLO11l (`yolo11l.pt`, imgsz 640,
conf ≥ 0.4).

## Install and run

Tested on Ubuntu with Python 3.11 and an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 12.

```bash
# 1. System packages (OpenCV, pulled in by Ultralytics, needs libGL)
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0

# 2. Python packages
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Preparation command (needs internet, run once, not timed, ~5 min):
#    downloads yolo11l.pt, builds the TensorRT FP16 engine yolo11l.engine
#    for THIS GPU, and checks the model loads
python prepare.py

# 4. The timed run (no internet needed)
python run.py --input <folder of .parquet files> --output results.jsonl
```

Optional flags (defaults are the tuned values):

| flag | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--workers` | half the CPU threads | decode processes |
| `--batch-size` | 64 | frames per GPU batch |
| `--sample-rate` | 3 | frames per second of video sent to the model (`0` = every frame) |
| `--backend` | `auto` | `auto` = the TensorRT engine if `prepare.py` built one, else PyTorch fp16; or force `tensorrt` / `pytorch` |
| `--fp32` | off | PyTorch backend only: float32 instead of float16 |

Progress and timing go to stderr every 15 s.

## How it works

```
reader thread ──video bytes──> decode workers ──frames──> GPU loop ──> results.jsonl
(main process)                 (N processes)              (main process)
```

1. **Reader** (`videoindex/parquet_source.py`) reads each Parquet file's
   `mp4` column once and queues the videos. A FineVideo file is a single row
   group, so reading per row would re-read the whole file each time.
2. **Decode workers** (`videoindex/pipeline.py: decode_worker`) decode every
   frame with PyAV (needed for exact timestamps) but convert only a sample of
   frames to images: the first frame in each 1/3-second slot. Frames with a
   rotation tag are turned upright. Each sampled frame is letterboxed with
   Ultralytics' own `LetterBox`, so the model sees exactly what `predict()`
   would give it. Frames travel to the main process through shared memory.
3. **GPU loop** groups frames of the same size into batches and hands them
   to a GPU thread, which runs YOLO11l as a **TensorRT FP16 engine**
   (`videoindex/trt_engine.py`, tuned for the common 640x384 input). The
   engine takes the letterboxed uint8 BGR frames directly: uint8 -> float,
   HWC -> CHW, BGR -> RGB and /255 are nodes inside the ONNX graph and so
   inside the engine. Then
   NMS (IoU 0.7, class-aware, conf > 0.4) for the whole batch in one call
   (`videoindex/detector.py: batched_nms_counts`, checked to give the same
   counts as Ultralytics' `non_max_suppression` by `tools/test_nms.py`).
   The main thread prepares the next batch while the GPU works.
4. **Per-second rules** (`videoindex/seconds.py`): an object is present if it
   was found in at least half of the second's sampled frames; the people count
   is the median, rounded down at a half. These are the brief's section 5
   rules, applied to the sampled frames.

Failures: a video that cannot be decoded gets one error line; a video that
fails partway keeps the seconds already decoded plus an error line; if a
decode process crashes, its video is reported and a new process replaces it.

## Checking correctness

```bash
python tools/test_rules.py        # per-second rules and frame sampling
python tools/test_rotation.py     # rotation matches ffmpeg (needs ffmpeg)
python tools/test_nms.py <file.parquet>   # batched NMS == Ultralytics NMS, on real frames
python tools/reference.py --input <folder> --output reference.jsonl   # every frame, plain predict()
python tools/compare.py results.jsonl reference.jsonl                 # the brief's three metrics
```

`tools/reference.py` is a deliberately plain version: every frame, one video
at a time, Ultralytics `model.predict` with its defaults. It is how the
fast version was checked (see `NOTES.md`).

## Files

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `run.py` | entry point |
| `prepare.py` | one-time download of `yolo11l.pt` and TensorRT engine build |
| `videoindex/` | the pipeline: reading, decoding, detection, per-second rules |
| `tools/` | reference, scorer and tests |
| `results.jsonl.gz` | results for the 50 FineVideo files |
| `HARDWARE.md` | where and how long the full run took |
| `WRITEUP.md` | answers to the write-up questions |
| `ai_chats/` | AI chat history |

# Video indexing at speed: FineVideo × YOLO11l

For every second of every video in a folder of FineVideo Parquet files, this
records which of **person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone** appear and how many
people are visible, using Ultralytics YOLO11l (`yolo11l.pt`, imgsz 640,
confidence 0.4, class-aware NMS at IoU 0.7).

## Install and run

Tested on Ubuntu with Python 3.11 and an NVIDIA driver that supports CUDA 12.
No CUDA toolkit is needed: PyTorch and TensorRT bring their own CUDA libraries
as pip packages.

```bash
# 1. System packages: OpenCV (installed by Ultralytics) needs libGL and glib
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0

# 2. Python packages (all 65 pinned to exact versions)
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Preparation command: needs internet, run once before the timed run,
#    takes about 5-9 minutes. It
#      - downloads the official yolo11l.pt next to run.py,
#      - exports it to ONNX with the input preprocessing built in,
#      - builds a TensorRT FP16 engine (yolo11l.engine) for THIS GPU,
#      - checks that the model loads.
python prepare.py

# 4. The timed run (no internet needed)
python run.py --input <folder of .parquet files> --output results.jsonl
```

The engine must be built on the machine that runs `run.py`: a TensorRT engine
only works on the GPU model it was built on. If the engine build fails, or the
engine cannot be loaded, `run.py` says so on stderr and falls back to PyTorch
fp16 automatically. The results stay correct; the run is slower (about 1.6x).

Optional flags (the defaults are the tuned values):

| flag | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--workers` | half the CPU threads | decode processes |
| `--batch-size` | 64 | frames per GPU batch (the engine accepts up to 64) |
| `--sample-rate` | 3 | frames per second of video sent to the model (`0` = every frame) |
| `--backend` | `auto` | `auto` = the TensorRT engine if present, else PyTorch; or force `tensorrt` / `pytorch` |
| `--fp32` | off | PyTorch backend only: float32 instead of float16 |

Progress and timing go to stderr every 15 seconds. Results go only to the
`--output` file.

## How it works

```
reader thread ──video bytes──> decode workers ──frames──> GPU thread ──> results.jsonl
(main process)                 (N processes)              (main process)
```

1. **Reader** (`videoindex/parquet_source.py`) reads each Parquet file's
   `mp4` column once and queues the videos. A FineVideo file is a single row
   group, so reading per row would re-read the whole file each time.
2. **Decode workers** (`videoindex/pipeline.py: decode_worker`) decode every
   frame with PyAV, because exact timestamps decide which second a frame
   belongs to, but convert only a sample of frames to images: the first frame
   in each 1/3-second slot. Frames with a rotation tag are turned upright.
   Each sampled frame is letterboxed with Ultralytics' own `LetterBox`, so the
   model gets exactly the input `predict()` would build (640x360 becomes
   640x384). Frames travel to the main process through shared memory.
3. **GPU thread** gets batches of same-size frames and runs YOLO11l as a
   **TensorRT FP16 engine** (`videoindex/trt_engine.py`). The engine takes the
   letterboxed uint8 BGR frames as they are: the uint8 to float conversion,
   HWC to CHW, BGR to RGB and /255 are nodes inside the ONNX graph, and so
   inside the engine. NMS then runs for the whole batch in one GPU call
   (`videoindex/detector.py: batched_nms_counts`), giving the same counts as
   Ultralytics' `non_max_suppression`. The main thread builds the next batch
   while the GPU works.
4. **Per-second rules** (`videoindex/seconds.py`): an object is present if it
   was found in at least half of the second's sampled frames; the people count
   is the median, rounded down at a half. These are the brief's section 5
   rules, applied to the sampled frames.

Failures: a video that cannot be decoded gets one error line; a video that
fails partway keeps the seconds already decoded plus an error line; if a
decode process crashes, its video is reported and a new process replaces it.
A video's timestamps start at its first decoded frame, as the brief defines.

## Why 3 frames per second is enough

The graders' reference runs the model on every frame. Running it on 3
evenly spread frames per second instead, and applying the same rules, was
measured against an every-frame reference built with plain Ultralytics
`predict()` (`tools/reference.py`) on 66 videos (4.3 hours):

| frames/s | objects F1 | people exact | people within 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.956 | 0.872 | 0.978 |
| **3 (default)** | **0.983** | **0.940** | **0.996** |
| 5 | 0.990 | 0.959 | 0.999 |
| thresholds | 0.95 | 0.85 | 0.95 |

Resampling the 66 videos into 1,000 random 13-hour test sets, 3 frames/s
still gives F1 ≥ 0.980 and exact ≥ 0.932 in 95% of them. An odd number of
samples also avoids a tie bias: with 2 samples, 1 of 2 already counts as
"at least half". Details in `NOTES.md`.

## Checking correctness

```bash
python tools/test_rules.py                # per-second rules and frame sampling
python tools/test_rotation.py             # rotation matches ffmpeg (needs: sudo apt-get install -y ffmpeg)
python tools/test_nms.py <file.parquet>   # batched NMS == Ultralytics NMS, on real frames
python tools/reference.py --input <folder> --output reference.jsonl   # every frame, plain predict()
python tools/compare.py results.jsonl reference.jsonl                 # the brief's three metrics
```

Only `tools/test_rotation.py` needs the `ffmpeg` command; `run.py` does not
(PyAV ships its own FFmpeg libraries).

## Files

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `run.py` | entry point |
| `prepare.py` | one-time download of `yolo11l.pt` and TensorRT engine build |
| `videoindex/` | the pipeline: reading, decoding, detection, per-second rules |
| `tools/` | reference, scorer, tests and benchmarks |
| `eval/` | the every-frame reference for the 66 evaluation videos, and the sweep script |
| `results.jsonl.gz` | results for the 50 FineVideo files |
| `HARDWARE.md` | where the full run was done and how long it took |
| `NOTES.md` | dated log of every measurement and change |
| `WRITEUP.md` | answers to the write-up questions |
| `ai_chats/` | AI chat history |

   frame with PyAV, because exact timestamps decide which second a frame
   belongs to, but convert only a sample of frames to images: the first frame
   in each 1/3-second slot. Frames with a rotation tag are turned upright.
   Each sampled frame is letterboxed with Ultralytics' own `LetterBox`, so the
   model gets exactly the input `predict()` would build (640x360 becomes
   640x384). Frames travel to the main process through shared memory.
3. **GPU thread** gets batches of same-size frames and runs YOLO11l as a
   **TensorRT FP16 engine** (`videoindex/trt_engine.py`). The engine takes the
   letterboxed uint8 BGR frames as they are: the uint8 to float conversion,
   HWC to CHW, BGR to RGB and /255 are nodes inside the ONNX graph, and so
   inside the engine. NMS then runs for the whole batch in one GPU call
   (`videoindex/detector.py: batched_nms_counts`), giving the same counts as
   Ultralytics' `non_max_suppression`. The main thread builds the next batch
   while the GPU works.
4. **Per-second rules** (`videoindex/seconds.py`): an object is present if it
   was found in at least half of the second's sampled frames; the people count
   is the median, rounded down at a half. These are the brief's section 5
   rules, applied to the sampled frames.

Failures: a video that cannot be decoded gets one error line; a video that
fails partway keeps the seconds already decoded plus an error line; if a
decode process crashes, its video is reported and a new process replaces it.
A video's timestamps start at its first decoded frame, as the brief defines.

## Why 3 frames per second is enough

The graders' reference runs the model on every frame. Running it on 3
evenly spread frames per second instead, and applying the same rules, was
measured against an every-frame reference built with plain Ultralytics
`predict()` (`tools/reference.py`) on 66 videos (4.3 hours):

| frames/s | objects F1 | people exact | people within 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.956 | 0.872 | 0.978 |
| **3 (default)** | **0.983** | **0.940** | **0.996** |
| 5 | 0.990 | 0.959 | 0.999 |
| thresholds | 0.95 | 0.85 | 0.95 |

Resampling the 66 videos into 1,000 random 13-hour test sets, 3 frames/s
still gives F1 ≥ 0.980 and exact ≥ 0.932 in 95% of them. An odd number of
samples also avoids a tie bias: with 2 samples, 1 of 2 already counts as
"at least half". Details in `NOTES.md`.

# Video indexing at speed: FineVideo × YOLO11l

For every second of every video in a folder of FineVideo Parquet files, this
records which of **person, car, dog, laptop, cell phone** appear and how many
people are visible, using Ultralytics YOLO11l (`yolo11l.pt`, imgsz 640,
conf ≥ 0.4).

## Install and run

Tested on Ubuntu with Python 3.11 and an NVIDIA driver for CUDA 12.

```bash
# 1. System packages (OpenCV, pulled in by Ultralytics, needs libGL)
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0

# 2. Python packages
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Preparation command (needs internet, run once, not timed, ~5 min):
#    downloads yolo11l.pt, builds the TensorRT FP16 engine yolo11l.engine
#    for THIS GPU, and checks the model loads
python prepare.py

# 4. The timed run (no internet needed)
python run.py --input <folder of .parquet files> --output results.jsonl
```

Optional flags (defaults are the tuned values):

| flag | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--workers` | half the CPU threads | decode processes |
| `--batch-size` | 64 | frames per GPU batch |
| `--sample-rate` | 3 | frames per second of video sent to the model (`0` = every frame) |
| `--backend` | `auto` | `auto` = the TensorRT engine if `prepare.py` built one, else PyTorch fp16; or force `tensorrt` / `pytorch` |
| `--fp32` | off | PyTorch backend only: float32 instead of float16 |

Progress and timing go to stderr every 15 s.

## How it works

```
reader thread ──video bytes──> decode workers ──frames──> GPU loop ──> results.jsonl
(main process)                 (N processes)              (main process)
```

1. **Reader** (`videoindex/parquet_source.py`) reads each Parquet file's
   `mp4` column once and queues the videos. A FineVideo file is a single row
   group, so reading per row would re-read the whole file each time.
2. **Decode workers** (`videoindex/pipeline.py: decode_worker`) decode every
   frame with PyAV (needed for exact timestamps) but convert only a sample of
   frames to images: the first frame in each 1/3-second slot. Frames with a
   rotation tag are turned upright. Each sampled frame is letterboxed with
   Ultralytics' own `LetterBox`, so the model sees exactly what `predict()`
   would give it. Frames travel to the main process through shared memory.
3. **GPU loop** groups frames of the same size into batches and hands them
   to a GPU thread, which runs YOLO11l as a **TensorRT FP16 engine**
   (`videoindex/trt_engine.py`, tuned for the common 640x384 input). The
   engine takes the letterboxed uint8 BGR frames directly: uint8 -> float,
   HWC -> CHW, BGR -> RGB and /255 are nodes inside the ONNX graph and so
   inside the engine. Then
   NMS (IoU 0.7, class-aware, conf > 0.4) for the whole batch in one call
   (`videoindex/detector.py: batched_nms_counts`, checked to give the same
   counts as Ultralytics' `non_max_suppression` by `tools/test_nms.py`).
   The main thread prepares the next batch while the GPU works.
4. **Per-second rules** (`videoindex/seconds.py`): an object is present if it
   was found in at least half of the second's sampled frames; the people count
   is the median, rounded down at a half. These are the brief's section 5
   rules, applied to the sampled frames.

Failures: a video that cannot be decoded gets one error line; a video that
fails partway keeps the seconds already decoded plus an error line; if a
decode process crashes, its video is reported and a new process replaces it.

## Checking correctness

```bash
python tools/test_rules.py        # per-second rules and frame sampling
python tools/test_rotation.py     # rotation matches ffmpeg (needs ffmpeg)
python tools/test_nms.py <file.parquet>   # batched NMS == Ultralytics NMS, on real frames
python tools/reference.py --input <folder> --output reference.jsonl   # every frame, plain predict()
python tools/compare.py results.jsonl reference.jsonl                 # the brief's three metrics
```

`tools/reference.py` is a deliberately plain version: every frame, one video
at a time, Ultralytics `model.predict` with its defaults. It is how the
fast version was checked (see `NOTES.md`).

## Files

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `run.py` | entry point |
| `prepare.py` | one-time download of `yolo11l.pt` and TensorRT engine build |
| `videoindex/` | the pipeline: reading, decoding, detection, per-second rules |
| `tools/` | reference, scorer and tests |
| `results.jsonl.gz` | results for the 50 FineVideo files |
| `HARDWARE.md` | where and how long the full run took |
| `WRITEUP.md` | answers to the write-up questions |
| `ai_chats/` | AI chat history |

# Hardware

The full 50 files were run on my own workstation (a shared lab machine).

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, 32 GB (driver 595.71.05) |
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, 16 cores / 32 threads |
| RAM | 121 GB |
| Disk | Samsung 990 EVO 2 TB NVMe SSD |
| OS | Ubuntu 25.10, kernel 6.17 |
| Python | 3.11 (conda env), torch 2.8.0+cu128, TensorRT 10.13.3.9 |

**Note: the GPU was shared.** During every run, other services on the
machine were using it: a vLLM engine (holding about 20 GB of memory) and a
live 4-camera detection pipeline with its Triton server (a steady 15-20% of
the GPU's compute, more at times). So these times are slower and noisier
than they would be on a dedicated GPU.

## Full run times (all 50 files: 1,650 videos, 128.3 h of video)

| version | wall time, start to finish |
|---|---|
| First working version (PyTorch fp16, 3 frames/s) | 3,603 s (60.1 min) |
| TensorRT FP16 + batched NMS + GPU thread | 1,014 s (16.9 min) |
| **Final version** (as above, with the preprocessing built into the engine) | **1,332 s (22.2 min)** |

`results.jsonl.gz` is the output of the final version's run.

The final version is not slower than the one before it: timed alternately on
the same batch, its engine is about 2% faster. Its full run happened while
the other services were loading the GPU more heavily; on the 66-video
evaluation subset the same code ran at 689 frames/s at that time, against
1,241 frames/s earlier in the day.

Each time is for `python run.py --input <folder> --output results.jsonl`
with the default settings (16 decode workers, batch 64, 3 frames/s), after
`python prepare.py` had built the TensorRT engine (an untimed one-off step of
5-9 minutes).

# SENDING process, so frames sent just before a worker exits can no longer
# be opened by the GPU loop (FileNotFoundError in rebuild_storage_fd).
# "file_system" uses named shared-memory files that outlive the sender.
# Must be set in every process, so it lives at import time of this module.
mp.set_sharing_strategy("file_system")

# Messages from workers to the GPU loop are tuples whose first item says what
# they are:
#   ("start",  worker_id, video_id)
#   ("frames", video_id, seconds_tensor, frames_tensor)
#   ("done",   worker_id, video_id, n_frames_sent, n_seconds, error_or_None)
#   ("exit",   worker_id)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Decode worker (runs in its own process)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def decode_worker(worker_id, tasks, results, sample_rate, chunk_size, decoder_threads):
    # Each process gets one core's worth of work; stop libraries from
    # starting their own thread pools on top of that.
    import cv2

    from .detector import make_letterbox

    cv2.setNumThreads(1)
    torch.set_num_threads(1)
    letterbox = make_letterbox()

    while True:
        task = tasks.get()
        if task is None:  # no more videos
            break
        video_id, mp4_bytes = task
        results.put(("start", worker_id, video_id))

        sampler = FrameSampler(sample_rate)
        chunk_seconds, chunk_frames = [], []
        frames_sent = 0
        n_seconds = 0
        error = None

        def send_chunk():
            nonlocal frames_sent, chunk_seconds, chunk_frames
            if chunk_frames:
                results.put((
                    "frames",
                    video_id,
                    torch.tensor(chunk_seconds, dtype=torch.int32),
                    torch.from_numpy(_stack(chunk_frames)),
                ))
                frames_sent += len(chunk_frames)
                chunk_seconds, chunk_frames = [], []

        try:
            for t, frame in iter_frames(mp4_bytes, decoder_threads):
                second = second_of(t)
                n_seconds = max(n_seconds, second + 1)
                if not sampler.keep(t):
                    continue
                image = letterbox(image=frame_to_bgr(frame))
                # A chunk must hold frames of one size; flush if the size changes.
                if chunk_frames and image.shape != chunk_frames[0].shape:
                    send_chunk()
                chunk_seconds.append(second)
                chunk_frames.append(image)
                if len(chunk_frames) >= chunk_size:
                    send_chunk()
            if n_seconds == 0:
                error = "no frames could be decoded"
        except Exception as exc:
            error = f"could not decode video: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}"[:200]

        send_chunk()  # frames decoded before an error are still counted
        results.put(("done", worker_id, video_id, frames_sent, n_seconds, error))

    results.put(("exit", worker_id))


def _stack(images):
    import numpy as np

    return np.stack(images)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reader thread (runs in the main process)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def read_parquet_files(files, tasks, results, n_workers, dispatched):
    """Queue every video for the workers, then one stop signal per worker.

    Rows that cannot be read are reported straight to the GPU loop as
    finished videos with an error.
    """
    for path in files:
        for video_id, mp4_bytes, error in iter_videos(path):
            dispatched.append(video_id)
            if error:
                results.put(("done", None, video_id, 0, 0, error))
            else:
                tasks.put((video_id, mp4_bytes))
    for _ in range(n_workers):
        tasks.put(None)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# GPU loop helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass
class VideoResult:
    """Everything known about one video while its frames are being counted."""

    frame_seconds: list = field(default_factory=list)
    frame_counts: list = field(default_factory=list)
    frames_counted: int = 0
    frames_expected: int | None = None  # known once the worker says "done"
    n_seconds: int = 0
    error: str | None = None
    crashed: bool = False  # its decode process died; no "done" will come

    def is_complete(self):
        return self.frames_expected is not None and self.frames_counted == self.frames_expected


class ShapeBatcher:
    """Groups incoming frames into batches of one image size.

    Frames from different videos can share a batch as long as their
    letterboxed size matches (most FineVideo videos are 640x360 -> 640x384).
    """

    def __init__(self, batch_size):
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.pending = defaultdict(list)  # shape -> [(video_id, seconds, frames), ...]
        self.counts = defaultdict(int)    # shape -> number of pending frames

    def add(self, video_id, seconds, frames):
        shape = tuple(frames.shape[1:])
        self.pending[shape].append((video_id, seconds, frames))
        self.counts[shape] += len(seconds)

    def full_batches(self):
        for shape in list(self.pending):
            while self.counts[shape] >= self.batch_size:
                yield self._take(shape, self.batch_size)

    def all_batches(self):
        """Everything still pending, including part-filled batches."""
        for shape in list(self.pending):
            while self.counts[shape] > 0:
                yield self._take(shape, self.batch_size)

    def is_empty(self):
        return not any(self.counts.values())

    def _take(self, shape, n):
        """Remove up to n frames of one shape. Returns [(video_id, seconds, frames)]."""
        items = self.pending[shape]
        taken, got = [], 0
        while items and got < n:
            video_id, seconds, frames = items[0]
            k = min(n - got, len(seconds))
            taken.append((video_id, seconds[:k], frames[:k]))
            got += k
            if k == len(seconds):
                items.pop(0)
            else:
                items[0] = (video_id, seconds[k:], frames[k:])
        self.counts[shape] -= got
        if not items:
            del self.pending[shape], self.counts[shape]
        return taken

The README, requirements and results are updated for the latest change. The next speed-up is built and checked for correctness, but I can't measure its speed until the GPU is quieter.

## What's on Beast's GPU, and what could be paused
| Service | GPU memory | Real compute | Effect of pausing |
|---|---|---|---|
| `3dvt-person-live-*` (4 cameras) + `triton-engine-1` | ~5.5 GB | **steady 15–20%, with swings** | **The main source of timing noise** |
| `vllm` | **20 GB** | ~0% idle, bursts when it gets requests | Frees memory and removes the bursts |
| clearml, label-studio, go2rtc, redis | none | none | Pausing these won't help |

The "100% utilisation" figure is misleading: it only means some kernel is always running. These are team services, so I haven't touched them. If you pause them, I'd need the GPU quiet for **about 40 minutes**: a clean speed comparison, then the final timed full run.
```bash
docker stop $(docker ps -q --filter name=3dvt-person-live) triton-engine-1 vllm
# afterwards: docker start <the same containers>
```

## Done
- **`requirements.txt`**: all 65 packages pinned, including everything Ultralytics pulls in, exactly as in the environment that passed the clean-install test.
- **`README.md`** rewritten. It covers the `sudo apt-get install -y libgl1 libglib2.0-0` step, what `prepare.py` does and how long it takes, that the engine is built for one GPU and that PyTorch takes over if it fails, why 3 frames per second is enough (with the measured table), and that `ffmpeg` is only needed for one optional test.
- **New engine everywhere:** `results.jsonl.gz` now comes from the new engine's full run (all 1,650 videos), and `HARDWARE.md` shows its 1,332 s with the shared-GPU explanation.

## Next speed-up: reusing results for near-identical frames
This is built and off by default (`--reuse-threshold`). About a quarter of sampled frames are near-copies of the previous one (static shots, slides).

| threshold | frames skipped | F1 | exact | within ±1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| off | 0% | 0.983 | 0.940 | 0.996 |
| 1 | 16% | 0.980 | 0.935 | 0.996 |
| 3 | 29% | 0.974 | 0.923 | 0.994 |

All pass, but each step costs a little margin. I couldn't measure the speed gain: the same no-reuse run took 43 s and then 61 s minutes apart because of the other jobs. On a quiet GPU, I'd expect threshold 1 to save about 10–15%.

**My recommendation:** if you can pause those services, I'll measure reuse properly, enable threshold 1 only if it clearly helps, and do the final timed full run, updating `results.jsonl.gz` and `HARDWARE.md`. If not, we submit as it is now, and that's already complete and verified.

"""Check that a stuck decoder or a failing reader cannot hang the run.

    python tools/test_robustness.py <folder of .parquet files (small)>

Two scenarios, each run in a fresh process with a 5-minute limit:

1. Time limit hit: VIDEO_TIMEOUT_SECONDS is set to 0.05 s, so workers are
   killed in the middle of videos, as a hung decoder would be. The run must
   finish, and every video must still have a line (its finished seconds,
   then an error line).
2. Reader failure: the Parquet reader raises after the first video. The run
   must still finish instead of the workers waiting forever.
"""

import json
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from collections import defaultdict
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent

SCENARIOS = {
    "time limit hit": """
import videoindex.pipeline as p
p.VIDEO_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 0.05
""",
    "reader failure": """
import videoindex.pipeline as p
real = p.iter_videos
def failing(path):
    for i, item in enumerate(real(path)):
        if i == 1:
            raise RuntimeError("simulated reader failure")
        yield item
p.iter_videos = failing
""",
}

RUN = """
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, {root!r})
{patch}
p.run(input_dir={input!r}, output_path={output!r}, workers=2, batch_size=64,
      sample_rate=3, device="cuda:0", half=True)
"""


def main():
    folder = sys.argv[1]
    for name, patch in SCENARIOS.items():
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            output = Path(tmp) / "out.jsonl"
            script = Path(tmp) / "scenario.py"  # a file, so spawned workers can import it
            script.write_text(RUN.format(root=str(ROOT), patch=patch, input=folder, output=str(output)))
            try:
                proc = subprocess.run([sys.executable, str(script)], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300)
            except subprocess.TimeoutExpired:
                raise SystemExit(f"FAIL {name}: the run hung")
            assert proc.returncode == 0, f"{name}: exit {proc.returncode}\n{proc.stderr[-2000:]}"

            lines = defaultdict(list)
            for line in output.read_text().splitlines():
                row = json.loads(line)
                lines[row["video"]].append(row)
            errors = {v: r[-1]["error"] for v, r in lines.items() if "error" in r[-1]}
            print(f"ok   {name}: finished, {len(lines)} videos have lines, {len(errors)} with an error line")
            for video, message in sorted(errors.items())[:3]:
                print(f"       {video}: {message}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Where does the time go inside one GPU batch?

    python tools/profile_batch.py <a .parquet file> [--batch 64] [--repeats 50]

Takes `batch` real letterboxed frames and times each step the GPU thread
does for a batch, with CUDA events (GPU time, not Python time):

  copy to GPU -> engine (preprocessing + YOLO11l) -> NMS + counting -> copy back

Reports the median over `repeats` batches, so short spikes from other jobs
on a shared GPU do not distort it.
"""

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import torch

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))
from videoindex.decode import frame_to_bgr, iter_frames  # noqa: E402
from videoindex.detector import Detector, batched_nms_counts, make_letterbox  # noqa: E402


def real_frames(parquet_path, n):
    letterbox = make_letterbox()
    column = pq.read_table(parquet_path, columns=["mp4"]).column("mp4")
    images = []
    for row in range(len(column)):
        for i, (_, frame) in enumerate(iter_frames(column[row].as_py())):
            if i % 10 == 0:
                image = letterbox(image=frame_to_bgr(frame))
                if not images or image.shape == images[0].shape:
                    images.append(image)
            if len(images) == n:
                return torch.from_numpy(np.stack(images))
    raise SystemExit("not enough frames of one size")


@torch.inference_mode()
def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("parquet")
    parser.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=50)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    detector = Detector()
    frames = real_frames(args.parquet, args.batch)
    print(f"backend {detector.backend}, batch {tuple(frames.shape)} uint8")

    steps = ["copy to GPU", "engine (preprocess + YOLO11l)", "NMS + counting", "copy back"]
    times = {step: [] for step in steps}
    with torch.cuda.stream(detector.stream):
        for repeat in range(args.repeats + 5):
            events = [torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) for _ in range(len(steps) + 1)]
            events[0].record()
            on_gpu = frames.to(detector.device, non_blocking=True)
            events[1].record()
            predictions = detector.model(on_gpu)
            events[2].record()
            counts = batched_nms_counts(predictions, detector._column_of_class)
            events[3].record()
            counts.cpu()
            events[4].record()
            torch.cuda.synchronize()
            if repeat >= 5:  # skip warm-up
                for i, step in enumerate(steps):
                    times[step].append(events[i].elapsed_time(events[i + 1]))

    total = sum(np.median(t) for t in times.values())
    for step, t in times.items():
        median = np.median(t)
        print(f"  {step:32s} {median:6.2f} ms  ({median / total:5.1%})")
    print(f"  {'total':32s} {total:6.2f} ms  -> {args.batch * 1000 / total:.0f} frames/s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

I've removed the reuse speed-up completely, found and fixed two problems in the current code, and profiled it. The final code still scores F1 0.983, exact 94.0%, within ±1 99.6% against the reference, the same as before.

## Problems found and fixed

Both were ways a single bad test file could **hang the whole run**, which the graders would stop at 6 hours:

1. **No time limit per video.** If the decoder froze on a corrupt file, `run.py` would have waited for it forever.
   - My first fix was wrong, and its test caught it. The main process killed a worker after 10 minutes, but a worker killed while sending frames leaves the shared queue locked, so every other worker then hangs too.
   - The final design has two levels. A worker checks the clock between frames and gives up on a video after **10 minutes** by itself, keeping the seconds it finished and adding an error line. Only a decoder that has been **frozen for 15 minutes** gets killed; a frozen worker isn't sending anything, so the kill is safe.
2. **If the Parquet reader hit an unexpected error**, the workers never got their stop signal and waited forever. Fixed.

[tools/test_robustness.py](tools/test_robustness.py) checks both by forcing a slow video, a frozen decoder and a failing reader. The run finishes in all three cases.

**The run doesn't need internet.** With every connection blocked and logged in all processes, `run.py` made **0 connection attempts** and its results passed.

## Profiling

It had only been done on earlier versions, so I redid it on the current code.
- **Inside one batch of 64 frames** ([tools/profile_batch.py](tools/profile_batch.py)): the engine (preprocessing + YOLO11l) takes **88%**, the copy to the GPU 11%, and NMS only **1%**.
- **Whole run (cProfile):** the main thread spends most of its time **waiting for the GPU** to accept the next batch.

So the pipeline is GPU-bound, and the cost is now essentially the YOLO11l model itself. The only cheap gain left is about 5% from a faster CPU-to-GPU copy. It's small enough that I'd only do it if you want every last bit.

- The README now covers the time limits and lists the new test and measurement tools. `NOTES.md` has the review and both profiles.

# Hardware

The full 50 files were run on my own workstation (a shared lab machine).

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090, 32 GB (driver 595.71.05) |
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, 16 cores / 32 threads |
| RAM | 121 GB |
| Disk | Samsung 990 EVO 2 TB NVMe SSD |
| OS | Ubuntu 25.10, kernel 6.17 |
| Python | 3.11 (conda env), torch 2.8.0+cu128, TensorRT 10.13.3.9 |

**Note: the GPU was shared.** During every run, other services on the
machine were using it: a vLLM engine (holding about 20 GB of memory) and a
live 4-camera detection pipeline with its Triton server (a steady 15-20% of
the GPU's compute, more at times). So these times are slower and noisier
than they would be on a dedicated GPU.

## Full run times (all 50 files: 1,650 videos, 128.3 h of video)

| version | wall time, start to finish |
|---|---|
| First working version (PyTorch fp16, 3 frames/s) | 3,603 s (60.1 min) |
| TensorRT FP16 + batched NMS + GPU thread | 1,014 s (16.9 min) |
| **Final version** (as above, with the preprocessing built into the engine) | **1,332 s (22.2 min)** |

`results.jsonl.gz` is the output of the final version's run.

The final version is not slower than the one before it: on the 66-video
subset the two took 37.5 s and 37.7 s, the same within noise. Its full run happened while
the other services were loading the GPU more heavily; on the 66-video
evaluation subset the same code ran at 689 frames/s at that time, against
1,241 frames/s earlier in the day.

Each time is for `python run.py --input <folder> --output results.jsonl`
with the default settings (16 decode workers, batch 64, 3 frames/s), after
`python prepare.py` had built the TensorRT engine (an untimed one-off step of
5-9 minutes).

## Full run times (all 50 files: 1,650 videos, 128.3 h of video)

| version | wall time, start to finish | GPU conditions |
|---|---|---|

| TensorRT FP16 + batched NMS + GPU thread | 1,014 s (16.9 min) | shared |
| **Final version** (as above, preprocessing built into the engine) | **1,127 s (18.8 min)** | live pipeline paused; vLLM serving requests |

`results.jsonl.gz` is the output of the final version's run. An earlier run
of the same final version, with every service active, took 1,332 s and gave
identical results.

For the final run the live camera pipeline was paused, but vLLM was serving
requests for much of it (about 1,300 prompt tokens/s at the start), so that
run still shared the GPU. Throughput moved between about 1,130 and 1,460
frames/s as vLLM's load changed. The previous version's 1,014 s run happened
to fall in a quieter period. On the 66-video subset the two versions took
37.5 s and 37.7 s: the same speed.

Each time is for `python run.py --input <folder> --output results.jsonl`
with the default settings (16 decode workers, batch 64, 3 frames/s), after
`python prepare.py` had built the TensorRT engine (an untimed one-off step of
5-9 minutes).
'''
s=s.replace(old,new); open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
cat >> NOTES.md <<'EOF'

## Final timed run (2026-11-22, 18:02-18:21 PKT)

All 18 3dvt-person-live containers were paused (`docker pause`, resumed by an
EXIT trap; runs/timed_run_paused_3dvt.sh). vLLM was NOT paused and was
serving requests (~1,300 prompt tokens/s at the start). Result: **1,127 s**,
EXIT=0, all 1,650 videos, no gaps or error lines, and identical to the
earlier 1,332 s run of the same engine (F1, exact, within 1 all 1.0000).
Throughput varied 1,130-1,460 frames/s with vLLM's load.
After resuming, the 4 imagebuffer containers had lost their RTSP streams and
were restarted by their restart policy; all stages back at 15 FPS.
EOF
